title: The petition
hook: here the one praying says why this Ardas is being made

segments.voice: Yesterday, honor of the humble, and your line: strength of the weak. Who did you stand with? Today, right after naming God that way, the Ardas finally says what it's for. Day six hundred thirty-three.

Sunday at the gurdwara. The congregation stands, hands joined, and the person leading the Ardas has been speaking for several minutes: the Gurus, the martyrs, the Khalsa, the gurdwaras far away, the good of everyone. Then the voice changes slightly. A name is spoken. A family's name, perhaps. A new baby. A grandfather's surgery next week. A shop opening on Main Street. A student leaving for college. For a few seconds, a prayer that belongs to a whole people becomes about one household's Tuesday.
screen: `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.` → `A FAMILY'S NAME IS SPOKEN.` → `ONE HOUSEHOLD'S TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: This is the petition, the part of the Ardas where the reason is named. Everything before it is fixed and shared. The opening invokes the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib. Then come the remembrances, the requests for the Khalsa and for the whole world, the line about the honor of the humble. Then, at this point, the one leading says something like: in Your presence, this Ardas is made for, and the reason is named in plain words. The congregation listens and joins the waheguru that follows. The word ardas itself is usually traced to a Persian word for a written petition, the kind a person would hand up to a ruler's court. That picture fits. A petition is not a speech. It's short, it's specific, and it names what is being asked. And notice who can be named. Not only the person leading. A family can ask the granthi to include their purpose: thanks for a safe journey, a new job, the anniversary of a death, a child's exam. At home, a person praying alone names their own reason the same way. Sikhs say the reason doesn't have to be grand. It does have to be honest. There's something steadying in that structure. The big, shared prayer holds a whole people's history. Then, inside it, your small reason is given a place, said out loud, in front of the Guru. Nobody is too small to have their reason named. And nobody's reason crowds out the good of all, because that part was said first.
screen: `THE FIXED PRAYER COMES FIRST.` · `THEN THE REASON IS NAMED.` · `ARDAS: A PETITION TO A COURT.` · `SHORT, HONEST, SPECIFIC.` · then, large: `SAY WHY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say your reason simply. Sit and let today's real concern rise. Not the one you think you should have. The one that's actually there. A worry, a hope, a thank-you. Now put it into one plain sentence. No flourishes. Just: this is for my mother's appointment. This is for the interview. This is thanks for the week. If you pray, you can say that sentence quietly to the One. If not, just let it sit in the open. The bell holds the time.
The petition. The moment in the Ardas when the reason for this prayer is named in plain words, inside a prayer that belongs to everyone.
Your line: say why. Today, when you ask someone for something, say the real reason in one honest sentence. Notice how it changes the asking. Day six hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, a family can ask the granthi to name their purpose in the Ardas, a birth, a journey, a remembrance; at home, the person praying names their own reason at the same point.

options: ask the granthi to name his surgery in the Ardas.
fork.reveal: families often ask for their purpose to be named. the shared prayer makes room for one household's need.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the standing prayer; often traced to Persian arz-dasht, a written petition.

trapdoor: what you thought: the whole Ardas is the same every time.
what it means: the fixed prayer holds a place where today's specific reason is named aloud.
what a scholar hears: ardas is usually derived from Persian arz-dasht, a petition presented to a court; the structure mirrors one: honor the ruler, then state the request plainly.

notes: Confirm the outline of the Ardas order given here (opening invocation, remembrances, requests, nimaaniaan de maan, then the specific petition) and the phrasing 'in Your presence, this Ardas is made for…'.
